Topology. The branch of mathematics studying spaces and continuity, focusing on properties that remain invariant under continuous deformation. Unlike geometry, which cares about distances and angles, topology asks only: which properties survive stretching, twisting, and bending without tearing or gluing? Born from Henri Poincaré's foundational work, topology bridges algebra, geometry, and analysis.

A topological space is a set X with a collection of open sets satisfying three axioms. The empty set and X are open. Finite intersections of open sets are open. Arbitrary unions of open sets are open. Continuous functions generalise from metric spaces to abstract topological spaces: a function is continuous if the preimage of every open set is open.

Homeomorphism is the topological equivalence. Two spaces are homeomorphic if there exists a continuous bijection with a continuous inverse. A classic example is that a coffee cup is homeomorphic to a torus—one handle—because one can be continuously deformed into the other without tearing.

Henri Poincaré founded algebraic topology, studying homology and homotopy groups, which are invariants that distinguish topological spaces and remain unchanged under homeomorphism. These tools allow us to classify spaces precisely.

A space is connected if it cannot be partitioned into two disjoint, nonempty, open sets. Connectedness is a topological property preserved under continuous images. In contrast, compactness, formalized by Heine and Borel, states that a metric space is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded. Compactness is also preserved under continuous images and has profound implications throughout analysis.

Knot theory, a subfield of topology, studies knots and links up to ambient isotopy—a purely topological classification that ignores how tightly or loosely a knot is tied. This gives a rigorous way to distinguish knots that cannot be continuously transformed into each other.

The fundamental group measures holes in a space. Spaces with different fundamental groups cannot be homeomorphic, providing a practical tool for distinguishing topological spaces. This invariant has become essential to classification in topology.

Hausdorff spaces axiomatize separation: any two distinct points can be separated by disjoint open neighborhoods. Many important spaces satisfy this condition, making it a useful property.

Continuity is the central concept of topology, which formalises which functions are continuous in abstract settings. The notion of a limit is fundamental to defining continuity and convergence in topological spaces. Set theory provides the foundational language of sets and functions upon which topology is built.
